entries.title: Abaddon
entries.summary: One of the two largest Godblood Zones on Earth, next to Kayaba Nationwide City.
entries.intro:
One of the two largest Godblood Zones on Earth, next to Kayaba Nationwide City. Described as the third most frenzied, terrible and unimaginable Godblood Zone on Earth.

  • Surrounded by sirens: human warning alarms that have never sounded. Their silence is part of the dread.
  • Its only outpost is The Rig.
  • Setting of the Abaddon (the game): the player operates from an outpost deep enough to meet terrifying things, but not the absolute worst.
unknowns: it is "the largest" and also "the third most" terrible. Not a contradiction (size vs danger) but worth stating clearly.

entries.title: Godblood Zones
entries.summary: Fragments of the dead gods' realms, left behind by the First Drowning, where Endro is so dense it can be seen.
entries.intro:
Fragments of god realms. They spilled from the Sea Before Time after the First Drowning, and the black fluid they left behind is Godblood, which gives them their name. **

  • Contain god emotions, so Endro is hugely present and visible as purple essence.
  • Home of Echoforms and other terrors.
  • The two largest on Earth flank Kayaba Nationwide City: Abaddon and Leviathan (Godblood Zone).
  • Many, of very varied size: dozens or more fragments of god realms; Abaddon and Leviathan are the largest, not the only ones.
  • Stable: fixed since the First Drowning. They do not grow, shrink or move; they are a geographic fact that society has adapted to.
  • The source also called them "veilzones". That colloquial term no longer fits the new name; an everyday short form is undecided.

entries.title: Godblood
entries.summary: The black, thick fluid of the First Drowning, shifting like a curtain of ink: the deluge of memory, dream and god-blood that the Sea sent into the mortal world.
entries.intro:
The black, thick fluid of the First Drowning, shifting like a curtain of ink: the deluge of memory, dream and god-blood that the Sea sent into the mortal world. The people of the time called it by the name of what it was, Godblood.

  • The places it left behind are the Godblood Zones.
  • **

entries.title: Kayaba Architecture and Look
entries.summary: How Kayaba Nationwide City looks and feels., correcting the first rewrite draft of Chapter 1, which pictured an ordinary city.
entries.intro: How Kayaba Nationwide City looks and feels., correcting the first rewrite draft of Chapter 1, which pictured an ordinary city.
entries.html:
Scale

  • Enormous in every direction. Not normal by any means. It is a dystopia.
  • A vertical city. Megastructures of 500 floors or more.
  • Sixty floors is nothing. A 60-story tower is a low building here.
  • People may live on floor 300 and never go down, or only go up a few floors. Life stays inside the structure.

Structure

  • Bridges between buildings.
  • Entire districts inside megabuildings: schools, pharmacies, malls, everything a life needs.
  • Like Kowloon, but more modern and not so poor.
  • Like Chinese films (dense, vertical, layered).

Materials and mood

  • Brutalist. Dystopian concrete buildings and glass.
  • Full of screens and advertisements.
  • Dark, oppressive and heavy; the weight of the structure is felt everywhere.

Technology

  • Futuristic, not neon. Technology is clean and integrated: architectural light lines in white or warm white, large screens, discreet projections, transit, drones, crowds. No neon, no cyberpunk colour signage.
  • But brutalist, not metallic. The base is raw concrete and glass; technology is applied onto the concrete as light, projection and screens. No chrome, no shiny metal panels, no spaceship surfaces.
  • Ads are real ads. A screen the size of a district shows a cheerful commercial face selling a product. The irony is a happy ad over a depressing city; the face itself is not sad (Chapter 1: "sold a smile to no one").

In the novel

  • Towers of 500+ floors, bridges threading the gaps, annex roofs, shafts meant for pipes; a canyon between towers with no visible bottom (Chapter 1).
  • Screens the size of a district sell the same smile everywhere; family names stand on the towers in letters ten floors tall (Chapter 1).
  • The roof of a tower: gravel, an access door, a shin-high concrete lip; the tower sways in the wind and the air is thin (Chapter 1).
  • The ocean lies to the east of the city; at dusk the towers' shadows stretch across it (Chapter 1).
unknowns: What is below: the lowest levels, the ground, the water?
How the megabuildings connect to the ocean and the harbors (about 30% of the city covers the ocean, Kayaba Nationwide City).
How an old city district such as Kobe fits into this vertical mass.

entries.title: Kayaba Nationwide City
entries.summary: A megacity that covers all of Japan and part of the ocean around it: 12.53 billion people in towers of five hundred floors and more.
entries.intro:
Population: 12.53 billion (year 2190). Setting of the novel's opening (Chapter 1).

  • No traditional farmland remains "in the wake of" The Singularity; not even mountains were spared.
  • It covers all of Japan's terrain plus ~30% of the surrounding ocean.
  • Divided into gigantic areas that were formerly cities (Tokyo, Nagoya, Kobe...) plus a handful of new ones. Each has its own culture, slightly changed over decades.
  • Huge population and bustling economy because it sits between the two largest Godblood Zones on Earth: Abaddon and Leviathan (Godblood Zone). Near them Endro is abundant.
  • Visible from the outpost the Abaddon (the game) is set in ("close enough to see Kayaba far away").

The name Kayaba is kept despite its resemblance to the Sword Art Online creator's surname.
entries.html:
How it looks

A vertical, brutalist megacity of concrete and glass, with megastructures of 500 floors or more, bridges between buildings and whole districts inside megabuildings. See Kayaba Architecture and Look.

The rest of the world

Other regions are also enormous. There are other megacities or large nations; Kayaba is the most famous, not the only one. The world's total population is roughly 30-40 billion. Which regions exist, who runs them and how they relate to Godblood Zones is undefined.

In the novel
info: All of Japan and about 30% of the surrounding ocean

entries.title: Kayaba Power and Society
entries.summary: Who rules Kayaba Nationwide City and how it lives.
entries.intro: Who rules Kayaba Nationwide City and how it lives.
entries.html:
Who governs

The clans of Shardwell holders rule above everything. The old bloodlines of holders (Inheritance) and the immortals of the deepest levels (Diving Index) are the real authority.

Clans and corporations

The corporations belong to the clans. The lineages founded or bought the corporations born from The Singularity. Capital is the new face of the old power. Consequence: the clans effectively steered the AGI era.

Food

No farmland remains, so food comes from several sources:

  • Synthetic or vertical production (Singularity technology).
  • The sea and the Godblood Zones (fishing, including the risky fishing at Abaddon).
  • Imports from other regions (Kayaba Nationwide City: other regions are also enormous).
  • Endro-derived food (an industry built on Endro or on altered creatures, Echoforms).

Harvesting Endro from people

Both legal and clandestine. There is an official market and a black one. The official side is presentable; the hidden side is brutal (Endro and Society).

The clans

Many mixed clans with crossed alliances, and some important clans that everyone knows. Lineages are mixed by marriage and pacts, so the opposition ring of the Sovereigns (Sovereignty and Domains) is lived as tension inside and between clans, not as five tidy houses.

The state

A bureaucracy that lives off crumbs. The police and administration exist but have little real power: they handle everyday life and the clans decide what matters.

Criminal syndicates

Both: independent powers with their own rules, and hidden branches of the clans. Some syndicates answer to a clan in secret; others negotiate with clans without belonging to them. Kalfu worked for one that used and discarded him.

The chip behind the eye

It does all four: identity and access; augmented view (it shows information, such as the existence of The Rig); tracking Endro and emotions; and surveillance and control for those in power. It is what lets harvesting and control exist at scale (Endro, Endro and Society).

Money

A dual system: currency and Endro. Ordinary people live on currency; the clans live on Endro. Because Endro is stable forever (Endro), the rich hold reserves for centuries. Inequality is structural.

Social classes

Four layers:

  1. The clans (blood nobility).
  2. Shardwell holders (free holders, by depth).
  3. Citizens (the masses, with the eye chip).
  4. The undocumented (those living outside the registry).

Kalfu and Hinata are at the bottom of this ladder.

Who owns the stolen technology

The corporation Kalfu robbed belongs to a minor, ambitious clan that bet on the beauty-district technology to rise. Kalfu stole its big chance; its power is fragile. Open: who ordered the theft (Kalfu, Endro and Society).

Consequences to keep in mind

  • Corporate crime and persecution (as in Chapter 1) are an expression of clan power.
  • The Rig was built by a corporation of the Singularity era, so it too belongs to a clan (The Rig).
  • The new technology that replaces Chrona holders threatens the clans' grip on youth (Endro and Society).

In the novel

  • The chip: a chip behind the left eye, put in at age six in Kalfu's case, draws a pale line at the edge of sight and never turns off. Whether it is universal is open.
  • Agents in grey with a small emblem at the collar chase Kalfu. They have no sirens and no papers and are not police. The emblem belongs to an organization still to define.
  • Police come with sirens and papers and end in a cell (Chapter 1).
  • Family names are written on the towers in letters ten floors tall: the old families own the buildings (Chapter 1).
  • Common belief that Shardwells belong to the old families is a folk belief that conflicts with the numbers;

(from the novel's consistency flags)

  • Shardwell holders: almost all common holders are registered and live outside ordinary neighborhoods; clans and corporations claim and recruit them early. The visible holders are the old families. How registration works (chip, tests, activation) is open. Consequence: if Kalfu's activation is detected, someone will come for him.
  • The chip: almost universal, implanted at six; the undocumented (the fourth layer) do not have one.
  • The agents in grey belong to a hired private security corporation; its name and who pays it are open.
unknowns: Education, districts and daily life; the exchange between currency and Endro.
Who ordered the theft, and the name of the minor clan.

entries.title: Leviathan (Godblood Zone)
entries.summary: The second of the two largest Godblood Zones on Earth, opposite Abaddon around Kayaba Nationwide City.
entries.intro: The second of the two largest Godblood Zones on Earth, opposite Abaddon around Kayaba Nationwide City.
entries.html:
Character

The domain of colossi. Creatures of titanic scale (the "Leviathan-Class Entities" of the Abaddon (the game)) live here: they change the weather and drag boats. Its threat is scale, not subtlety. All of them are Echoforms.
unknowns: Whether anyone has outposts or routes there; what its geography looks like.
Why the two largest zones sit on either side of Japan.
How it contrasts with Abaddon, where the human settlement of The Rig exists.

entries.title: The Rig
entries.summary: The biggest man-made, oil-rig-like megastructure; the only outpost in Abaddon.
entries.intro:
The biggest man-made, oil-rig-like megastructure; the only outpost in Abaddon.

  • Surrounded by an invisible force field that keeps it invisible from outside. The only way to detect it is to crash into its massive legs.
  • Its population has a free electronic chip behind the eye, the only way to know it is a megastructure (the chip reveals it).
entries.html:
It is the game's outpost

It is the outpost of the Abaddon (the game): the sizeable settlement where the player lives and sells, deep enough in Abaddon to meet terrifying things. From inside you can see Kayaba Nationwide City far away; from outside the Rig is invisible.

Origin

Built by a corporation from the era of The Singularity, to harvest Endro and exploit the zone. It began as a corporate asset and became a community.

Who lives there

A mix: workers and fishers, fugitives, and corporate staff. A microcosm of Kayaba's layers: owners above, workers in the middle, exiles below. The invisibility draws people who want to hide (like the protagonist of Chapter 1, if the story takes him there; not stated).

Factions

The Rig has factions with reputation that the player can raise (in the game they unlock things such as themed clothing sets). Which factions exist is not defined yet.
info: A corporation of the Singularity era
unknowns: Which factions exist and what each one wants and offers.
Which corporation, who owns it today, the exact population (the source sentence is cut off).
How buyers find it (the eye chip is the only way to know it exists) and what flows between the Rig and Kayaba.
Why the force field exists, what powers it, and its relation to Endro.

entries.title: The Singularity
entries.summary: not an AI that acts on its own.
entries.intro:
not an AI that acts on its own. The Singularity is the birth of AGI and the immense, constant technological change it set in motion, steered by the corporations that used it. It is a process and an era, not a being or a single catastrophe.

  • It reshaped Japan into Kayaba Nationwide City: no traditional farmland remained, not even mountains were spared.
  • It explains the high-tech texture: the eye chip, force fields, the vertical city, megastructures such as The Rig.
  • Corporate power is therefore at the root of the modern world, which ties directly to the theme of exploitation and inequality.
  • Do not confuse it with The Primarch, also described as "a singularity".
unknowns: When AGI was born and how long the transformation took.
Which corporations led it and who owns the AGI now (or whether AGI is now many systems).
How it relates to Endro: did AGI discover it, harvest it, or run on it?

entries.title: Hinata
entries.summary: Younger sister of Kalfu.
entries.intro: Younger sister of Kalfu.
entries.html:
Details

  • Age: pre-teen, 10 to 13 (exact age pending). The adults-only rule for sexual content applies.
  • Family: her mother died when she was a child; her father was always absent and she doesn't know him (Kalfu).
  • Personality: luminous and stubborn, tender, tsundere, lovable. Also very intelligent: nothing slips past her. She knows exactly what is happening and knows how to handle herself.
  • Kalfu fights so she keeps studying.

Why she matters

  • She is the reason he is the way he is. His wrong belief that she is better off without him is the thing she would see through immediately (Kalfu).
  • She contrasts with the dark world: her name and her light are the counterweight.
  • She may carry a shard from the same father (49% inheritance, Inheritance). Not decided.

In the novel

  • Seen only in Kalfu's memory: a low table in a kitchen too small for two, a lamp that is always on, a tablet in her hands, one sock half off; she does not look up.
  • She says: "You're late. I wasn't waiting. I was studying. Both can be true." She leaves a warm plate under an upturned bowl.
unknowns: Exact age, appearance, school and where they live.
What exactly she knows about her brother's crimes and about their father.
Whether she carries a shard.
Her voice and how tsundere shows in her speech without becoming a stereotype.

entries.title: Kalfu
entries.summary: Protagonist of the novel (Chapter 1).
entries.intro: Protagonist of the novel (Chapter 1).
entries.html:
Details

  • Name: Kalfu. It is his real name. He is Japanese, of unmixed blood.
  • Age: 17. He is the protagonist of the novel; his age only matters for the content rule that sexual content involves adults only.
  • Background: a precarious worker of Kayaba Nationwide City, one of the exploited masses.
  • Work: he worked for criminal "corporations", bandit syndicates like the Yakuza, always doing crimes.
  • The mission: they sent him on one more mission "as always". He found out that this time they had made him steal something very important: a new technology inside the beauty district, which replaces the Chrona-domain holders who give visual youth (Diving Index, Endro and Society). They already wanted to get rid of him.
  • Family: a younger sister, Hinata (pre-teen, 10-13), and no one else. He fights so she keeps studying. His mother died when he was a child. His father was always absent.
  • His father: an important person who slept with his mother. Neither Kalfu nor his sister knows this. All they know is that their father was never present. This is how Kalfu has a Shardwell (Inheritance: the shard passed from the father).
  • What pushes him to the roof: he feels disposable; he fears decades in prison; and he believes his sister will be better off without him.
  • How he got to the roof: he was not climbing stairs. He was doing parkour through the megastructure until he found himself trapped on the top floor. The roof is a dead end, not a choice of route (Kayaba Architecture and Look).
  • At the end of Chapter 1: he jumps from a tower, his Shardwell activates and the Initial Displacement begins. He did not know he had one; it had formed and lay dormant.

Personality

Dry, with dark humor; quiet and observant; protective even if he denies it. The street taught him to read people; his thoughts are richer than his words; he defends himself with bitter irony (the thoughts in Chapter 1); behind the hardness is care for his sister and for the weak, which comes out in spite of himself.

Want

Nothing: he starts empty, and that changes. He has no desire of his own at the start; the Shardwell and the story give him one. His arc is recovering the ability to want something. (His wound, feeling disposable, is why the want is gone.)

Pursuers

The corporation he robbed (the beauty-district corporation), after the technology. It belongs to a minor, ambitious clan that bet on that technology to rise (Kayaba Power and Society). He sits at the bottom of Kayaba's four classes (the undocumented or the masses, not decided). His own syndicate's role in setting him up remains part of the backstory (Chapter 1).

Appearance

Agile, athletic body; he is always on the run, so he is flexible. Good-looking and attractive. (He is 17: describe his looks naturally, never in a sexualized way, Content Boundaries.) Hair, eyes, height and style pending.

Fears

  • That Hinata is left alone.
  • That his life never mattered.
  • Water and falling. A physical fear that his decision to jump directly contradicts, which makes the moment on the roof carry more weight (Chapter 1).

Flaws

  • He doesn't ask for help and doesn't let himself be helped.
  • He distrusts everyone.
  • He lies to protect.
  • He erases himself: he considers himself expendable and decides for others without asking.

Home

Kobe, one of the old cities that make up Kayaba Nationwide City (a port city, near the sea).

Role

Kalfu is **the protagonist of the novel Shardwell** (Shardwell Novel), the only novel that exists so far.

Implications

  • The stolen technology threatens the value of Chrona-domain holders and the people who profit from their service (immortals, corporations). That is why someone wants him dead and why the technology is worth a corporation's pursuit.
  • His sister may also carry a shard: the same father, 49% inheritance per child (Inheritance).
  • If the father is important and carries a shard, he may be one of the powerful: a clan member, a corporate figure or a Diver. Not decided.

In the novel

  • Cannot swim; nobody in his district can. The ocean is "something you look at from above" (Chapter 1, Common Knowledge).
  • A chip behind his left eye since age six draws a pale line at the edge of his sight and never turns off. Inside the trial it shows nothing (Chapter 1, Chapter 2).
  • Moves by parkour; his hands are torn open from a six-hour run; he has spent years learning not to fall (Chapter 1).
  • Believed wells were for the old families, "not for people like him" (Chapter 2). He recognized the first dive from common knowledge.
  • He remembers a classroom poster with the five Sovereign names and a rhyme; he only remembers that Chrona was "the one with the clocks" (Chapter 2, Five Sovereigns).
info: Water and falling; that Hinata is left alone
unknowns: What the technology does exactly, who owns it, and what it needs (does it use Endro?).
Who the father is, and whether he knows he has children.
His hair, eyes, height and clothes; his voice and how he speaks.
What his empty state looks like in daily life, and what first reawakens a desire.
Which Sovereign's shard he carries and the concept of his Dominion (Sovereignty and Domains, Edicts).
Whether the word "Yakuza" is used or the syndicates get an in-world name.

entries.title: Body and Mind Changes
entries.summary: Descending changes the diver's body and mind.
entries.intro: Descending changes the diver's body and mind. People who were fully human can become something else. This is the permanent cost of depth (Diving, Diving Index). Visible traits can appear from Rippleborn (level 1); Undertow (level 3) brings the first deep, irreversible change; the Sea of Mirrors is where "the self dissolves".
entries.html:
What decides the form

A mix, and sometimes unpredictable. The diver's psyche, the concept of their sovereignty (Edicts) and the imprint of the dead Sovereign (Five Sovereigns) all play a part, and the result cannot be fully predicted. This gives variety and risk.

How far it goes

Strong, but still a person. Identity and social life remain. The author's examples:

  • Enormous people, translucent skin, eyes that look like a universe.
  • Demon horns, animal traits, tails, and cat-girls and similar beings.
  • "More chill" anime-style looks, or wilder and stranger ones.

Changes are visible, so they are a public sign of who someone is.

How society sees them

  • Admired and envied. A visible change means the person has a Shardwell and is more powerful, so an ordinary human is below them by default.
  • Exploited by the powerful. People in power take advantage of those with less power. That includes mundanes and weaker Shardwell holders.
  • Not framed as discrimination against the changed. The hierarchy runs on power.

Author statement

Rippleborn can show visible traits such as cat ears, tails, scars, Endro marks and eyes with effects. Varied animal traits (cat, wolf, fox, rabbit and more), demon horns and antlers are confirmed for Rippleborn in the game; in Abaddon they are chosen, not grown.
unknowns: Relation to Echoforms (do deep Divers resemble them?).
Whether changes are heritable (Inheritance).
Exact rules: how fast, at which levels, can they be hidden or reversed.

entries.title: Diving Index
entries.summary: The depth of the connection between soul and shard.
entries.intro:
The depth of the connection between soul and shard. Pairs with Hierarchy Levels, the title of a person at that depth.

#LevelMeaningHierarchy title
1RippleFirst contact between the soul and the divine fragmentRippleborn
2CurrentMoves within shallow waters; deepening the connectionDrifters
3UndertowA hidden pull drags deeper. First deep, irreversible change (Rippleborn may already show visible traits)Undertaken
4Streamborne VeinCurrents of the "Sea from before time" flow inside themStreamborne
5DescentThe true dive begins; past the comfort zone; one is testedDescender
6Abyssal CrownA "minor god" in perception; still mortal, mythically powerfulAbyssals
7Hadal DepthLowest point before divine contact. Unlocks gifting shards (Inheritance)Hadal Ones
8Sea of MirrorsThe point where the self dissolvesFathomers
9The Primarch's BreathThe deepest, unreachable layerPrimarch's Heirs

The one-to-one pairing of levels and titles is **Names kept as written.

Shape of the pyramid: very steep. Nearly all Shardwell holders stay near the top (Rippleborn, Drifters). Reaching Abyssal Crown is for thousands of people worldwide, so immortals are a tiny elite.

From Abyssal Crown (6) a person can sustain more than one shard (Sovereignty and Domains).

Progression is a continuous descent (Diving), not separate exams; levels are depth bands. Each level costs the diver something permanent: Body and Mind Changes.

Related: Diving, Initial Displacement, Sea Before Time, The Primarch. Immortality: it begins at Abyssal Crown (6). Historical figures alive today were discarded, so immortals are invented characters.

  • Most immortals do not look old. They can ask someone with a Chrona (time) domain for visual youth. That service has value in a beauty economy (Endro and Society).
  • Open: how many Abyssals exist and how many are ancient; whether Chrona holders can restore youth only or also age others.

entries.title: Diving
entries.summary: Going down through a Shardwell toward the drowned heart of its Sovereign. The body stays behind, unconscious.
entries.intro:
Going down through a Shardwell toward the drowned heart of its Sovereign. This is how Edicts and Tithes are earned and how a person climbs the Diving Index / Hierarchy Levels.

  • Outside of the first dive, time flows the same inside as outside.
  • The first dive is special: Initial Displacement.
entries.html:
Mechanics

  • The body stays, unconscious. Only the consciousness descends. The body is left vulnerable outside, so divers need protection, safe places and care. This makes guards, clinics and trust part of diving.
  • Death inside: the person is not dead outside. The body is left empty, in a coma. A lost diver is alive and unreachable, which raises questions of long-term care and a possible economy of the "lost".
  • Progress is one continuous, progressive descent, not a series of separate exams. The nine levels of the Diving Index are depth bands along that fall. Some points are one-way (Undertow: "the first irreversible step").
  • Trials come from the bearer, reflected by the shard (Initial Displacement); the gods are dead (Five Sovereigns).

What depth gives

  1. More Dominion: wider, deeper reach over the concept (Edicts).
  2. More Endro capacity (Endro).
  3. More powerful Tithes.
  4. Changes in body and mind: the permanent cost. See Body and Mind Changes.

Common knowledge (established in the novel)

Ordinary people know that some who dive never finish and are found afterward "still breathing, with no one in them" (Chapter 2, Common Knowledge).
unknowns: Surfacing: a diver can wake mid-descent and resume only at certain points (rest points). Outside those points there is no way back.
Open: where the rest points are, how long a descent takes outside, and what makes a coma permanent.

entries.title: Edicts
entries.summary: A Dominion is the portion of a Sovereign's law that a shard gives its bearer, over a concept the bearer chooses (the author's example: gravity).
entries.html:
Dominion: what you gain

A Dominion is the portion of a Sovereign's law that a shard gives its bearer, over a concept the bearer chooses (the author's example: gravity). The Sovereign's Domain is the whole law (time, space, void, order, life); a Dominion is a person's piece of it (Sovereignty and Domains, Five Sovereigns).

  • It comes from the shard and deepens by Diving: more reach over the concept.
  • The same concept can be reached through different Domains with a different flavor (Sovereignty and Domains).

Edicts: what you do

An Edict is a use of a Dominion that the person invents themselves. Like a sovereign issuing a decree, the bearer decides what their authority over the concept does.

Nothing is restricted. Edicts are not a list of skills you collect. A person with a Dominion over gravity can invent uses that would never occur to anyone else; two people with the same Dominion will use it differently.

  • It stays scientific: an Edict is an action created and performed by the person. Example: "Feather Fall" is someone controlling matter and moving the air upward around their body.
  • Each Edict requires Endro, inside and outside the Shardwell. The cost varies with the use. Spent Endro transforms into the effect.
  • First Edicts are simple (Initial Displacement).
  • Counterpart: Tithes (objects).

Why it matters

  • Creativity is the skill ceiling, and where readers can theorize possibilities.
  • Limits come from what the concept physically allows, from the Endro cost, and from opposed Domains (Sovereignty and Domains), never from a fixed list.
unknowns: Whether "Edict" and "Dominion" appear in everyday speech or only among Divers.

entries.title: Endro
entries.summary: Energy made from emotion. It powers every Shardwell, Edict and Tithe, and near the Godblood Zones it can be seen as purple haze.
entries.intro: The heart of the power system. Energy and food for the Shardwell and anything connected to it. Needed for Edicts and Tithes, inside and outside the Shardwell.
entries.html:
What it is

  • Chemical residue from reactions in the brain when feeling emotions. It floats around beings with emotions and physically exists.
  • Hybrid nature: inert in ordinary places (a particle-like residue), but near Godblood Zones it clusters into cell-like structures. This explains the denser Endro, the purple haze and the greater number of Echoforms where Endro is concentrated.
  • Near Godblood Zones it is hugely abundant (god emotions) and visible as purple essence.
  • Spending: spent Endro transforms into the effect (heat, motion, force). Nothing is lost; it is converted, as in physics. Implication: Endro is convertible to energy, so its quantity per effect needs a scale.
  • Production: any being with emotions produces it (humans, animals; Shardwell holders are not special). The amount depends on the intensity of the emotion, and the type of emotion changes the Endro (each emotion yields a different "flavor").
  • Storage: stable forever. It can be stored indefinitely, so reserves and hoards can last centuries.
  • Still undefined: what each emotion's Endro does differently; whether flavors have affinity for Sovereign domains (Sovereignty and Domains); what makes it cluster; the Endro-to-energy scale.

Using it

  • Guiding Endro to a Shardwell is the fastest way to activate or grow it: Shardwell Activation, Inheritance.
  • Living through extreme events can also activate a Shardwell, just slowly, because the Endro is not guided.
  • Endro can be stored, gathered and sold: see Endro and Society.
  • Cells may carry information on the emotions behind them: see Endro Memory and Mind Abilities.

Used in the game: Abaddon (the game) (Endro density map, absorbers, granades).

entries.title: Inheritance
entries.summary: In Classical Antiquity 100% of humans absorbed a shard and formed a Shardwell.
entries.html:
Base rule

In Classical Antiquity 100% of humans absorbed a shard and formed a Shardwell. By 2190 only ~1-2% have one. For that to work, the chance a child inherits from a parent is ~49%. It does not stack: same chance even if both parents have one.

Math check: with a world of ~30-40 billion (Kayaba Nationwide City), 1-2% means roughly 300-800 million holders, about 1.4-2.8 times the ~250 million people of antiquity. That works if each holder has about 2.5 or more surviving children at 49% each, which is plausible; it does not require holders to disappear. Fewer holders would mean fewer children per holder.

Children of multi-shard holders

Someone with several shards (Sovereignty and Domains) passes on at most one shard, chosen at random among those of the parents. The 49% rule still applies and does not stack. Lineages therefore stay tied to a single Sovereign, even if a parent holds several.

Bypass: Hadal Depth

A person who reaches Hadal Depth (Diving Index) can choose any mundane person and make them form a shard of choice (or several). Only shards the giver possesses can be gifted.

  • Slow: the new shard must first be created by the Hadal One, a process similar to mitosis, costing huge amounts of Endro.
  • A newly inherited shard takes ~1 year to form a Shardwell naturally. Guiding Endro into it speeds this up greatly (Shardwell Activation).

Families tend to carry the same god's shard for 2,000+ years, so most people know which god's shard they hold (Initial Displacement).

entries.title: Initial Displacement
entries.summary: The first dive, which can only happen once, when the Shardwell is activated for the first time (Shardwell Activation).
entries.intro:
The first dive, which can only happen once, when the Shardwell is activated for the first time (Shardwell Activation).

  • Time outside appears paused; the dive happens "so fast".
  • Where the first Edicts and Tithes are gained. They are very simple: swords, tools, objects, small abilities. (The source sentence is unfinished: "something akin to...")
  • Most people already know which god's shard they hold (the family has inherited it for 2,000+ years), so they have an idea of what to expect.
  • It is the first trial of the gods. It depends entirely on who is challenging and which god hosts it. It is made for the challenger so it can be completed, and is the only stage that can be non-deadly.
  • Who makes the trial: the bearer themself, reflected by the shard. The gods are dead (Five Sovereigns); the trial comes out of the diver's own psyche and the shard only materializes it. This is why each trial is made "just for them" and fits the Sea of Mirrors (Diving Index). To resolve: what the dead god's imprint contributes (theme, shape, difficulty).

Rank reached: Ripple / Rippleborn (Diving Index, Hierarchy Levels).
entries.html:
In the novel

  • Common knowledge: when a Shardwell wakes you go inside and the world outside stops for you; the first dive can be finished; it is made for the one who goes in; some never finish and are found breathing, with no one in them.
  • The trial Kalfu enters: a clean, empty, silent vertical city under a fixed white sun and a blue sky, with ribbons of water falling sideways through the air, streams down the towers and clear water that rises (Chapter 2, Novel Plan - Act 1).
  • Inside the trial: hours pass for him (he tires and climbs) but the sun never moves; his eye chip shows nothing.

entries.title: Shardwell Activation
entries.summary: For a formed Shardwell, the straightforward method: guide Endro into it.
entries.intro:
For a formed Shardwell, the straightforward method: guide Endro into it. Feel Endro essence around you (or stored somewhere) and direct it to the Shardwell; eventually it activates.

Alternative: extreme life events can activate it too, but slowly, since the Endro is not guided.

First activation triggers the one-time Initial Displacement.

entries.title: Shardwell
entries.summary: A hollow abyss formed when a shard of a Sovereign embeds in a soul: a "well" (the name comes from the shard inside it and its well nature).
entries.intro:
A hollow abyss formed when a shard of a Sovereign embeds in a soul: a "well" (the name comes from the shard inside it and its well nature). It leads down to the drowned heart of that Sovereign and, ultimately, to the Sea Before Time.

  • Origin: The Fracturing of the Sovereigns
  • Fuel: Endro
  • Gains from it: a Dominion over a concept, used through Edicts, and Tithes (objects)
  • How it is passed on: Inheritance
  • How it wakes: Shardwell Activation
  • How one goes deeper: Diving · Diving Index · Hierarchy Levels
  • Someone who has just awakened one is a Rippleborn.

The setting rule: everything makes sense scientifically. Powers are things the person does, not magic labels. See Edicts.
info: A shard of a dead Sovereign
The drowned heart of its Sovereign

entries.title: Sovereignty and Domains
entries.summary: How the Five Sovereigns connect to what a person can do.
entries.intro: How the Five Sovereigns connect to what a person can do.
entries.html:
Types of sovereignty

Five, one per Sovereign: Chrona (time), Vast (space), Nyther (void/entropy), Axion (order/law), Anastasis (life/renewal). A shard gives a portion of a law, and the bearer chooses the concept within it (e.g. gravity). Nothing is restricted; each person invents their own uses (Edicts).

The pentagon of opposition

Each Sovereign opposes the two neighbors in the ring:

Chrona ⟷ Vast ⟷ Axion ⟷ Nyther ⟷ Anastasis ⟷ Chrona

PairReason
Chrona ⟷ VastTime versus space, the classic duality
Vast ⟷ AxionBoundless expanse versus the order that confines
Axion ⟷ NytherOrder versus entropy
Nyther ⟷ AnastasisVoid and decay versus life and renewal
Anastasis ⟷ ChronaRenewal undoes the arrow of time and its decay
  • Opposition in practice: the effects of holders of opposed domains cancel or clash.
  • Non-opposed neighbors (the other two): affinity with nuances. They boost each other for some concepts and stay neutral for others, depending on the concept chosen.
  • Shared concepts, different flavors: a concept can be reached from several domains and behaves differently in each (e.g. gravity under Vast vs under Axion).
  • The Black Veil opposes all five equally. It sits outside the ring: the five oppose each other but all stand against it.

How clashes are decided

A mix of three factors: depth (Diving Index), Endro committed (Endro) and how well each side understands their concept. No fixed formula; each scene is resolved by causal logic.

The Sovereign's imprint

Besides the domain, the dead Sovereign leaves an imprint (Five Sovereigns) that contributes:

  • Theme and flavor of the trials (the bearer still creates the trial; the Sovereign colors it) (Initial Displacement).
  • A tendency in body changes (Body and Mind Changes).
  • Emotional roots / personality leanings, which also shape the Endro a lineage produces (Endro).

Several shards

  • A person can sustain more than one shard only from Abyssal Crown (level 6) on (Diving Index).
  • Combining opposed domains is possible and is the most powerful thing there is, but almost nobody manages it. Aspiration and mystery.
  • To explain: opposed effects cancel or clash, so holding opposites must be an internal clash that only extreme control can turn into power.
  • Several shards means several independent Shardwells: one well per shard, each descended separately. More cost, more time and more danger.
unknowns: Which concepts sit under which domains, with examples of each flavor.
Exactly what "cancel or clash" means: equal depth cancels? the deeper wins? what remains?
Which concepts have affinity between neighbors and which are neutral.
How a shard's domain shapes lineages (Inheritance) and the changes of the body (Body and Mind Changes).

entries.title: Tithes
entries.summary: Weapons, tools and objects obtained while Diving.
entries.intro:
Weapons, tools and objects obtained while Diving. They cannot be created normally: they are offerings from the gods. Creating one requires deep knowledge of how existence works, of the cosmos itself.

  • Need Endro to be spawned and used, inside and outside the Shardwell. Cost depends on the Tithe and may be nearly zero.
  • Early Tithes (Initial Displacement) are simple: swords, tools, objects.
  • Inspired by "Memories" in Shadow Slave; the same in theory.
  • Counterpart: Edicts.
  • Source: with the gods dead, Tithes are not "offerings" from a living god. They are materialized by the shard out of the diver's own trial (Initial Displacement). The name stays, reinterpreted: "Tithe" is the memory of a religion whose gods are dead. What the descent gives back to the diver is still called a Tithe, as a relic of that belief.

entries.title: Echoforms
entries.summary: Creatures from the Sovereigns' realms that wandered into reality during the First Drowning.
entries.intro: Creatures from the Sovereigns' realms that wandered into reality during the First Drowning. They haunt the drowned lands and Godblood Zones.
entries.html:
Classification idea (concept)

Echoforms can be identified by how they look and what they can be guessed to do, then grouped with similar ones.

Example: Endro/Telekinesis type. An entirely purple entity, a mass of purple haze. Categorized as able to use, store and steal Endro. Possible behaviors: compacting Endro into spheres and firing them as projectiles at huge speed; with telekinesis, crushing human heads with ease.

A simple visual description is enough to generate countless Echoforms this way.

Scope

Every creature altered by a Godblood Zone counts as an Echoform, from strange fish to titanic beasts. There is one taxonomy. The Abaddon (the game) loot tiers (Endro-infused fauna, aberrant organisms, Leviathan-class) are all Echoforms of increasing severity.

Still to define: what separates the tiers physically, whether new Echoforms can arise, and whether a creature leaving a zone stays an Echoform.

See also loot tiers in the Abaddon (the game) (tier 2-4 fauna are Endro-warped creatures; relation to Echoforms is not fixed).

entries.title: Black Veil
entries.summary: A thing without shape or will that drifted in from beyond the Sea Before Time.
entries.intro:
A thing without shape or will that drifted in from beyond the Sea Before Time. Not life, not death, but erasure: wherever it passed, truths unraveled. It did not kill; it unwrote.

  • The Five Sovereigns fought it with the laws of existence themselves: bound it in tides of time, drowned it in roots of impossible metal, shattered it in storms of entropy. It devoured even the rules that sought to bind it.
  • It cannot be destroyed, only denied. The only refuge beyond its reach is mortal souls, which are anomalies, not fixed into reality's fabric. This is why the Sovereigns hid inside them: The Fracturing of the Sovereigns.
  • The war continues, "indifferent to these fragile flickers of life".

Not to be confused with Godblood. The name overlap is a worldbuilding thread worth deciding on.
entries.html:
Status in 2190

Only a myth to ordinary people. The world does not know it exists; only the very deep (Hadal and beyond) know the truth, and the reader discovers it with them. Whether the Veil is still out there and what it does now is undefined.

Relation to the Sovereigns

The Veil opposes all five Sovereigns equally. It sits outside their ring of opposition: the five oppose each other, but all stand against it. See Sovereignty and Domains.

Where it is now

Deliberately left open. Not even the author has decided where the Veil is or what state it is in today. Treat it as an unresolved mystery of the story, not an omission.

entries.title: First Drowning
entries.summary: When the Sovereigns were gone their realms collapsed into the Sea Before Time, which overflowed into the mortal world by the Primarch's will.
entries.intro:
When the Sovereigns were gone their realms collapsed into the Sea Before Time, which overflowed into the mortal world by the Primarch's will.

Not merely a flood of water but a deluge of memory, dream and god-blood:

  • Lands warped. Seas that should not exist appeared overnight.
  • Time staggered and broke in drowned places.
  • Creatures from the Sovereigns' realms wandered into reality (Echoforms).
  • Whole coastal nations swallowed in hours; rivers flowed backward and drowned inland kingdoms.
  • Drowned lands became impossible to map: shifting, unreal, haunted by Echoforms.

The waters were black and thick like ink, called Godblood. The places it left behind are the Godblood Zones.

When: early humanity, when kings and emperors still existed, "when Rome was still a thing". Survivors named it "First" because they feared there would be more.

See Timeline.
entries.html:
What people know

Every child knows the story: when the gods broke, the sea came back; it came once and drowned the world. People who lived afterward called it the First Drowning because they were afraid there would be a second (Chapter 2, Common Knowledge).
info: Early humanity, the age of Rome
The Sea overflowed by the Primarch's will

entries.title: Five Sovereigns
entries.summary: The five gods that held up reality: Chrona, Vast, Axion, Nyther and Anastasis. They shattered themselves, and they are dead.
entries.intro: Born from the currents of the Sea Before Time at the Primarch's will. Each embodies fundamental laws of existence. Together they created the scaffolding upon which reality was built.
entries.html:
Domains

The five domains mix physical pillars of reality and abstract laws. The meanings of the names are intentional.

SovereignDomainOpposesNotes
ChronaTimeVast, Anastasisbound the Black Veil in "tides of time"
VastSpace, scale, void of distanceChrona, Axionnot yet detailed
NytherVoid / entropy / the unseenAxion, Anastasispossibly "storms of entropy"
AxionOrder / law / structureVast, Nytherpossibly "roots of impossible metal"
AnastasisLife / renewal / rising againNyther, Chronanot yet detailed

All five stand against the Black Veil.

Relationships and how they work with shards: Sovereignty and Domains.

Fate

Unable to destroy the Black Veil, they shattered themselves into countless shards that fell into mortal souls: The Fracturing of the Sovereigns. Each shard became a Shardwell leading to the drowned heart of its Sovereign. Their realms collapsed into the Sea, causing the First Drowning.

Every Shardwell holds a shard of one god; families inherit the same god's shard for millennia (Inheritance, Initial Displacement).

Status of the Sovereigns

Dead. Only echoes remain. The shards are remnants of power and memory, not living minds. The bottom of a Shardwell is a divine graveyard; the gods cannot answer, help or speak. trials and Tithes are produced by the bearer, reflected by the shard (Initial Displacement, Tithes). Still open: what the god's imprint contributes.

What people know

  • The five names (Chrona, Vast, Nyther, Axion, Anastasis) are on a classroom poster with a rhyme children sing to remember them. The rhyme is not written yet.
  • Common belief: the gods are dead and the wells lead to where they died. Kalfu recalls only that Chrona "was the one with the clocks".

-

entries.title: Sea Before Time
entries.summary: A boundless ocean of raw possibility, unshaped and eternal, existing beyond all known law.
entries.intro:
A boundless ocean of raw possibility, unshaped and eternal, existing beyond all known law. It predates the universe.

  • In its depths rested the The Primarch.
  • From its currents rose the Five Sovereigns.
  • After the Sovereigns shattered, their realms collapsed back into it, and it overflowed into the mortal world: the First Drowning.
  • Fragments of god realms that spilled out of it are the Godblood Zones.
  • Descending through a Shardwell leads toward it; see Diving Index.

entries.title: Shardwells in History
entries.summary: The shards fell during Classical Antiquity, so in human terms Shardwells are ancient.
entries.intro:
The shards fell during Classical Antiquity, so in human terms Shardwells are ancient. Early on, progress was slow: people did not know the shards were paths to godhood, nor that they came from real gods.

  • Some killed themselves in fear of becoming something, of illness, of "the mark of the devil".
  • Some were killed in experimentation, compared against dead bodies that had absorbed no shard.
  • Most found their way into the Shardwell by accident, only to be killed inside it.
  • Most called it the god's judgement, or the devil's infection.

Related: Shardwell, Diving Index, Inheritance, Timeline.

entries.title: The Fracturing of the Sovereigns
entries.summary: The Five Sovereigns realized the Black Veil could not be destroyed, only denied.
entries.intro:
The Five Sovereigns realized the Black Veil could not be destroyed, only denied. Souls were the one refuge: unpredictable, unbound, "born of the chaos between creation and destruction".

In their final act the Sovereigns shattered themselves into countless shards. The shards fell like rain into the mortal world and embedded deep in living souls. Each became a hollow abyss, a Shardwell, leading down to the drowned heart of its Sovereign.

Fell during the Classical Antiquity era; see Shardwells in History and Timeline. Followed by the First Drowning.

entries.title: The Primarch
entries.summary: A singularity resting in the depths of the Sea Before Time, containing all matter, all energy, all space and all time in a state beyond mortal comprehension.
entries.intro:
A singularity resting in the depths of the Sea Before Time, containing all matter, all energy, all space and all time in a state beyond mortal comprehension.

  • At its will the Sea stirred and the Five Sovereigns rose.
  • By its will the Sea overflowed into the mortal world: the First Drowning.
  • The deepest, unreachable layer of the Diving Index is The Primarch's Breath; the final hierarchy rank is Primarch's Heirs (Hierarchy Levels).
entries.html:
Will

The Primarch has a real, hidden intention: the overflow of the Sea (First Drowning) was deliberate. What that intention is has not been decided.

The name Primarch is kept despite its use in Warhammer 40K. "The Primarch's Breath" and "Primarch's Heirs" keep their names.
info: Singularity in the Sea Before Time
unknowns: is the Primarch a being with intent, or a force? The source gives it "will" but nothing more.

entries.title: Timeline
entries.summary: Only anchors given in the source.
entries.intro:
Only anchors given in the source. Dates are not set; everything between is open.

  1. Before the universe: Sea Before Time, The Primarch, Five Sovereigns.
  2. Age Before Tides: war against the Black Veil; mortal realm appears as an anomaly; civilizations rise and fall (flyers by will, ageless ones, cosmos-benders undone by "unnameable force").
  3. The Fracturing of the Sovereigns: shards fall during Classical Antiquity (Shardwells in History).
  4. First Drowning: early humanity, Rome era. Birth of Godblood Zones.
  5. Centuries of hidden/slow progress: fear, experimentation, deaths (Shardwells in History). In antiquity ~100% of humans absorbed a shard (Inheritance).
  6. The Singularity: reshapes Japan into Kayaba Nationwide City. (date unknown)
  7. Year 2190: present of the story. ~1-2% of humans have a Shardwell. Population of Kayaba: 12.53 billion.
unknowns: nothing between steps 5 and 6 (medieval to modern age). Historical figures alive today were discarded, so this gap has to be filled with real history of Shardwell holders: clans, institutions, how the world developed.

entries.title: Dead End
entries.subtitle: Chapter 1
entries.summary: The sun cast uncountable shadows across the ocean, and to him they felt like the bars of a cell.
entries.intro:
The sun cast uncountable shadows across the ocean, and to him they felt like the bars of a cell.

They stretched so far it seemed they could touch the orange horizon, but it was only a trick, played by a million towers and a sinking sun. The sight should have been remarkable. One could only wonder how it looked from the other side—what the ocean saw.

He had never learned to swim. Nobody in his district had. The ocean was something you looked at from above.

He had been running for six hours. This was where the running ended.

He had come up through the tower the only way left to him: over the bridges, across the annex roofs, through shafts meant for pipes and not for people, always up, because every way down had been closed behind him. His hands were torn open. He could not remember where. All he knew was that this was the last floor. Above him there was nothing but sky.

Behind him the city never ended. Concrete, then glass, then concrete, five hundred floors and more, until the haze took it. Bridges threaded the gaps between the towers. On the face of the nearest, a screen the size of a district sold a smile to no one, and under it a family name stood in letters ten floors tall, the kind of name that was a building before it was a person.

At the edge of his sight, the chip behind his left eye drew its pale line, as it had every day since he was six. It never turned off. It had never occurred to him that it could.

Even though it wasn't dark yet, a new light flickered to life every so often.

Up here, the city was gone. No footsteps. No horns. Nothing. Only the wind, shrill and relentless. Each breath came faster, harder, and was not enough. The air was too thin.

Why bother breathing so hard?

The building swayed like a pendulum. The wind howled and clawed at him, as if it meant to take him away.

Maybe the wind will do it for me.

His legs shook, and he let them.

Behind him, nobody spoke. Nobody had spoken since the door.

He did not regret being here. He had come through the whole structure to reach this roof, and he wasn't about to gift the wind—nor them—a victory. If he was going to die, it would be with his own two hands. His choice.

Am I really that eager to die?

The thought hung there. He had come all the way up for exactly that.

Why did his feet suddenly feel so heavy?

Does anything matter anyway?

If he decided against it now, it wouldn't change anything. They were not police. Police came with sirens and papers, and ended in a cell. These had no sirens. These had no papers. What waited behind him would not look like a sentence. It would not look like anything.

His hair danced in time with the wind, his clothes barely clinging to him. He dragged his feet, never lifting them, as if the rooftop itself were the only anchor keeping him from the sky.

One step. And another. And another.

He looked back.

Seven of them, in the same grey, pressed into the lee of the access door where the wind could not reach. A small emblem was stitched at each collar. Their faces showed nothing, as if something had been poured into them and left to set. A coat snapped like a flag. No one moved. They did not step onto the gravel. The wind would have taken any of them in three paces, and they knew it.

They watched. They only had to wait.

He turned away. It cost him nothing. They were not people he could speak to.

A gust almost took him. His feet stayed planted. He inched forward against it until the roof ran out.

The edge was a low lip of concrete, no higher than his shin, slick with cold. He set his toes against it.

Beyond it, nothing. A canyon between towers, and in the canyon no bottom. Bridges, thin as threads. Screens glowing floor after floor, the same smile repeating itself down into the dark until the light simply gave up.

He had spent years learning not to fall. It was the one fear his body had never let go of.

His heartbeat scattered. His mind blurred with it. A wild exhilaration surged through him, tangled with dread.

He held his breath.

Sky.

Then not sky.

Wind in his mouth, in his eyes, in the hollow where his stomach had been. Something enormous went by: glass, a smile, a smile, a smile, too fast to be anything. His arms were somewhere. The world turned over, and he could not tell which way was down, and then he could, because it was coming.

A bridge. A light. Concrete streaming past like water.

Oh shit.

The thought arrived alone, small, and everything else in him went quiet around it.

He had jumped. He had actually jumped.

He remembered a lamp.

A low table in a kitchen too small for two. A lamp that was always on. A girl with one sock half off and a tablet glowing in her hands, who did not look up. You're late, she had said. I wasn't waiting. I was studying. Both can be true. A plate under an upturned bowl, still warm.

She'll be better off.

It was the last thing he had told himself on the way up. Only now, with nothing under him, did he hear it for what it was.

The fall went on.

Kalfu.

Her voice, from a night that was not here. Nobody else said it like that, the way you say the name of something you mean to keep.

Something clenched low in his abdomen, hard, as if a hand that had always been inside him had finally closed. Pain coiled outward, deep and old, and the whole night held its breath.

The roof was once again desolate.

entries.title: Still Water
entries.subtitle: Chapter 2
entries.summary: Water.
entries.intro:
Water.

It hit him from every side at once. No sky, no wall, no down. Cold in his mouth, in his eyes, in the gaps of his clothes. He kicked, and nothing pushed back. He did not know which way the air was.

He had never learned to swim.

Up. Which way is up.

There was light somewhere, a bright smear, and he went toward it with his arms and his whole body, and his lungs were on fire, and then something broke and there was air.

He coughed. His hand slapped at nothing, then at something: concrete, smooth, with a lip he could hook his fingers over. He dragged himself onto it and lay there, spitting water, shaking.

The water was clear.

That was the first thing his mind could hold. Clear as glass, down and down, and under him the towers kept going: windows, floors, bridges, sinking into blue until the blue went dark. A city, with the water already in it.

He rolled over and looked up.

It was noon.

That was wrong. He had jumped at dusk. He could still feel the orange of it on his skin. Now the sun stood small and white in a sky of perfect blue, without a single cloud, and the light fell on towers he almost knew. The same kind of concrete and glass, hundreds of floors, on every side. But clean. No stains. No cracks. The screens on the walls were blank and white.

High above the bridges, water fell across the sky in long clear ribbons, slowly, sideways, from nowhere to nowhere. Streams ran down the faces of the towers, along the seams of the concrete, floor after floor.

There was no sound. Not wind. Not machines. He heard his own coughing, barely, and the city gave nothing back.

He pressed a hand to his eye, out of habit. The chip behind it showed him nothing. No hour. No signal. No pale line at the edge of his sight that had been there since he was six. For the first time in his life, the only thing inside his head was him.

This is not the city.

Something low in his stomach was still closed, tight, a fist that had not opened. He knew what it was. Everyone knew. It was a story told in classrooms and at funerals and by drunk uncles about somebody's cousin: the well. The Shardwell. The first dive. When it woke, you went inside, and the world outside stopped for you. Wells belonged to the old families, the ones with names on the towers. Not to people like him.

It woke. It's in me. This is inside.

He said it again until it stopped sounding like a joke. Inside. Somewhere under the world, in the place the old gods had left behind when they died.

The stories said the first dive could be finished. The stories said it was made for the one who went in. They did not say what finishing was. They did not say who had made it. They said some people never finished, and were found afterward, still breathing, with no one in them.

He looked at the water. It lay quietly against the concrete an arm's length from his hand, clear and harmless.

He stood. He backed away from it. He put his hands on the wall.

Up.

It was what his body knew. A ledge, a pipe, a seam. Up was away from the water, and away from the water was the only direction that made sense.

He had been climbing for hours.

He did not know how many. The sun had not moved. That was how he knew it had been hours: he had watched it, over and over, waiting for it to lean, and it stayed exactly where it was, small and white and high, as if someone had pinned it there.

Chrona.

The word came from nowhere, from a poster on a classroom wall. Five names in a row, and a rhyme the children sang to remember them. Chrona, Vast, Nyther, Axion, Anastasis. He could not remember what any of them were for. Chrona was the one with the clocks.

Is this yours, then?

Dead gods did not do things. That was the other thing they said. So who?

The names turned over in his head like coins in a pocket, and meant nothing, and he kept climbing.

A ledge, then a pipe, then a bridge cable as thick as his waist, then another ledge. His hands were open and raw. He crossed a gap he should not have been able to cross, and did not think about it. He had stopped counting floors at three hundred. Every floor was the same. The same clean concrete, the same empty windows, the same stream of water running down the same seam. No stains. No fingerprints. A city this size should have smelled of people. It smelled of nothing.

A foothold gave. The streams had made the concrete slick, and his left foot went out from under him, and for one terrible heartbeat there was nothing under him at all. His fingers caught. His body swung. He hung over hundreds of floors with his whole weight on four torn fingers, his mouth open and no sound coming out.

He had spent years learning not to do this.

He pulled himself up. His arms shook. He did not look down. It was the only rule he had left.

At last the cable ended in a wide platform of poured concrete, flat, sheltered by a deep overhang. It stood at the edge of the tower, and here the city ended. His legs stopped on their own. He stood there with his hands hanging open and his chest working, and for the first time since the water, he was not moving.

To the east, past the last towers, lay the coast.

He knew it. It was the same ocean he had watched from the roof, the same one whose long shadows had looked like bars. It went all the way to the horizon, flat and bright, the same blue as the sky, without one wave. It did not look like the same ocean. It looked like a floor.

The city began to ring.

It started far below, a single low note, and then it was everywhere. Every pane of glass, every pipe, every seam in the concrete taking up the same pitch, until the whole city hummed like the rim of a glass. His own breath came back to him from three directions. His own heartbeat came back from the walls.

And under the hum, something else.

Water. Not falling. Moving. Something enormous turning over in its sleep.

He looked down.

The towers fell away beneath him in ledges and bridges and blank white screens, hundreds of floors, narrowing into a canyon. At the bottom of the canyon, so far down it was only a color, lay the water. Clear. Perfectly still. A single bright mirror at the bottom of the world, holding a small copy of the sky.

It had not moved. He had been climbing away from it for hours, and it had not moved. Out past the towers the ocean had not moved either.

Then the water moved.

A shiver crossed the mirror at the bottom of the canyon, from wall to wall, as if something under it had breathed in. And then it began to rise. Not like a flood, spilling and spreading. It rose whole, flat and level, climbing the towers like a floor in a lift, and every window it reached went blue, and full, and gone. Floor. Floor. Floor. Each one took it in a breath.

It climbed the tower below him. And the next one. And the next. All of them at once, a thousand windows drowning in order, and he heard nothing, because the sound was slower than the water and was still on its way.

And the ocean rose with it.

He saw it happen to the whole coast at once. The flat bright floor that ran to the horizon lifted, in one piece, slowly, and the horizon, which had been a line, began to climb the sky.

A floor a breath. Two. Four.

No.

Every child knew the old story. When the gods broke, the sea came back. It came once, and drowned the world, and the people who lived afterward called it the First Drowning because they were afraid there would be a second.

This is the second.

The canyon was gone. The city was disappearing from the bottom up, as though someone were erasing it.

His fingers closed on the edge of the platform. The torn skin split. He did not feel it.

The roar arrived.

It hit him from below, from everywhere, the sound of an entire city and an entire ocean being lifted, and the platform shook under his feet. The water was climbing the tower beside him now, close enough to see the foam, a hundred floors beneath him and rising.

He ran.

He went up the cable, the wall, whatever the structure gave him. He did not stop again. He did not look down again. He did not need to. It was the only sound in the world, and it was behind him.

Far above, past the last bridge, a single door stood in the face of a tower. It was lit from the inside.

It was the only thing in the whole bright city that cast a shadow.

entries.title: Wrong Distance
entries.subtitle: Chapter 3
entries.summary: The door did not get closer.
entries.intro:
The door did not get closer.

He had been climbing toward it for what felt like an hour, hand over hand up the faces of the towers, and it hung above him exactly as it had when he started: a small rectangle of light in a wall of grey. Same size. Same height. Same distance.

That's wrong.

He kept his eyes on it and climbed. Fifty floors. Sixty. He counted them out loud because there was no one to hear it. And little by little, the door grew. It took the shape of a door. He could see the frame.

Then his left hand missed the next hold, and he looked down at it for half a second.

When he looked up, the door was small again.

He hung there, breathing. His torn fingers burned.

He tried it again. He fixed his eyes on the door, and the door came closer, and the moment he looked away it fell back to where it had been, as if it had never moved. Distance did not hold when he was not watching it. It slid back the instant he stopped.

That made no sense. He said it again anyway, until it was something he could climb with.

The trouble was that he could not climb without looking at his hands. Every hold, every ledge, every seam he had to see to grab. If he watched the door, he could not see where to put his fingers. If he watched his fingers, the door ran away.

So he did both, badly. He looked at the door, and looked at the wall, and looked at the door, and the wall, a few seconds each, and the door crept closer in jerks, like something being dragged. His foot slipped once. A sliver of concrete broke off under his shoe and fell away, and he did not hear it land.

The water was behind him. He could not see it from here, but he could hear it. A deep sound, constant, patient, rising and falling the way a chest does.

He reached a bridge and crawled onto it, and for the first time he was able to look at something other than the wall.

The city lay around him in every direction.

It went on. It never ended. Tower after tower, bridge after bridge, ribbons of water falling sideways through the blue. He had known that already. But now he looked at it properly, and something was wrong with how it went on.

Those two towers. The tall one and the broken-topped one. I saw them an hour ago.

He turned. Behind him, in the other direction: the same two towers. The same bridge between them. The same three waterfalls, one long and two short, at the same distances.

He looked to the left. The same.

The city did not go on. It repeated. It was one stretch of towers, stamped over and over until the haze stopped it, and the haze was not far. At the edge of everything he could see a thin line where the blue of the sky met the grey of the concrete, and there was no horizon beyond it. It was a seam.

A room.

The thought was small and very cold. It was not a city. It was a room, and someone had made it look enormous.

To the east, past the towers, the ocean stood up.

He had looked away from it on purpose. Now he made himself look. It was not flat anymore. The whole sea had lifted, and the horizon no longer lay along the bottom of the sky but climbed it, a long bright wall of water that stood at the edge of the world and grew taller each time he blinked. It had not reached the city yet. It was still very far.

It was coming.

He checked his hand against the nearest tower. Then, because he could not help it, he checked the door. It sat in the grey wall, small, a rectangle of light, far.

I can't be here.

Through an empty window beside the bridge he saw a room. A desk, a chair, a wall. A clock above the desk.

The clock said noon.

He went to the next window. A clock. Noon. The next. Noon. He did not need to look at the sun to know what it would say.

Chrona. The one with the clocks.

It came back to him, the rest of what his teacher had said, one afternoon when he was ten and not listening. The five gods were not people, she had said. They were rules. The rules the world was built on. When the gods broke, the rules came loose, and the wells went down to where they had come loose. She had said it the way you say a thing to keep children away from a hole in the ground.

Chrona kept the clocks. And the one after her, Vast, something to do with distance, or size, or how far. The rhyme went too fast there. He could not remember the other three.

So this is what it looks like when the rules come loose.

He understood, then, that the sun was not broken. The clocks were not broken. The distance was not broken. They were doing exactly what they were meant to do, in the wrong way.

The sound of the water changed.

He had stopped to think. Of course he had. He had been sitting on a bridge, in the sun, with his chest heaving, thinking, and the sound he had been hearing for an hour as a murmur was a roar now, rolling up the towers, nearer, much nearer. A low note rang in the glass.

He stood. He ran.

The sound thinned. It sank back to a murmur by the time he reached the end of the bridge.

He stopped again, just for a breath, and the roar returned, and the glass rang, and he ran, and it went away.

It's only when I stop.

He said it aloud, and his voice came back to him from the towers, thin and strange.

It only comes when I stop.

He did not know why. He did not know what stopping was, to this place. But he knew now what kept it behind him. As long as he was moving, it stayed where it was. The moment he rested, it came.

So he did not rest.

He climbed. He watched the door, then his hands, then the door, then his hands, and he did not stop, and the roar behind him became a murmur and a murmur became a pulse. The sun did not move. The clocks said noon. The towers around him were the same towers. Every time he looked away from the door it fell back, and every time he looked at it again it came closer, and the gap between the two kept getting smaller, a hair at a time.

At last it was above him. Not far. A rectangle of light in a plain grey wall, on a narrow ledge, with the water falling past it in a thin bright sheet.

It was a steel door. Scratched. Ordinary. It had a handle, and the handle was worn smooth in the middle where a hand had held it many times. Its shadow lay long and black on the wall behind it, though the sun stood straight above him.

He pulled himself up onto the ledge. He had nothing left. His fingers did not close properly.

He put his palm flat against the door.

It was warm.

Not warm like metal in the sun. Warm like something that had been leaning against the other side.

entries.subtitle: The game
entries.summary: Ideation from the source doc.
entries.intro: Ideation from the source doc. All conceptual; nothing is final.
entries.html:
Visual direction

  • Models inspired by PS2–PS3 era, with lower-res textures where the pixels are visible.
  • Plants are pixelated images on bent planes; hair follows the same logic (cards, not 3D strands). No voxels.
  • Mix of PS2 and modern: the sea and effects are crisp and high-quality (not pixelated), with an old-school aesthetic; pixels live in models and their textures.
  • Inspired by Nivalis (moody city, unfiltered textures, atmosphere) but clearly distinct.
  • Built on Max's own engine; technical plan lives outside this vault (D:\Obsidian Vault\Abaddon Development).

Players and platforms

  • Single-player, co-op, and local servers of up to 24 players.
  • PC Windows + Steam Deck, designed for controller.

Player character

  • The player creates their own character, highly customizable: from petite and cute to an old bearded man; cute, emo, rough styles. Always adults.
  • Faces: semi-realistic PS2 style, not anime.
  • All playable characters are Rippleborn and never level up (deeper levels are for future games).
  • Rippleborn traits available: ears and tails (cat, wolf, fox, rabbit and more), demon horns, antlers, scars, Endro marks, eyes with effects. Chosen at creation, changeable later; they do not grow during play (see Body and Mind Changes).
  • Factions with reputation in The Rig; reputation unlocks themed cosmetic sets and possibly more. Which factions: pending.
  • For now: clothing is cosmetic only, no crafting, no real-money purchases, no gameplay reactions on marks/eyes.
  • Cosmetics: clothing and items bought in The Rig or found while playing.

Fantasy

"You're alone and have one of the worst jobs." You are a Rippleborn (Diving Index): able to use Endro equipment, have Endro-type senses, very thinly connected to your Shardwell.

Loops

  • Base: Exit home → go to boat → undock → ride to desired zone → fish/loot → ride back → dock → sell → buy upgrades/progression → repeat.
  • Simple: Ride → Loot → Ride → Sell/Progress → Repeat.

Core mechanics

Fishing · Navigation · Upgrading boat · Upgrading/buying tools · Upgrading abilities.

Setting

  • Main economy hub: a sizeable outpost close enough to see Kayaba Nationwide City far away, deep enough in Abaddon to meet terrifying things, not deep enough for the absolute worst. This outpost is The Rig.
  • No other islands or outposts nearby: the only land the player knows, plus weird encounters and architecture to explore.
  • NPCs are not a main feature; seen doing their thing here and there to sell isolation.
  • Falling in the ocean does not kill: the player can swim and even see underwater. Whether the water should still be feared, and what makes it dangerous, is pending.

Equipment

Navigation / boat: map with Endro density · Endro density meters (upgrade) · upgradable hull to withstand high Endro · Harpoon · 5 invisibility Endro granades (refilled daily) · powerful net for small swarms · Endro absorbers · fishing rod. Other: bait granade · invisibility reactor · sound siren. Main fishing gear: rod, harpoon, boat net.

Loot and encounters

  • Absorb Endro with the boat's absorber upgrade.
  • Normal fish → rod. Small swarms → net. Bigger creatures → harpoon (kill/capture). Dangerous ones → evade with invisibility granade.
  • Events that don't kill (may reward) and events needing player input (may reward).

Rippleborn abilities the player can use

Damage Endro granades · fire harpoon with Endro · sense/fear powerful creatures nearby · absorb Endro.

Loot tiers (ChatGPT suggestion, in the source)

  1. Shallow Catch: safe fish, low gain, stable.
  2. Endro-Infused Fauna: slight visual abnormalities, occasional aggression, moderate profit.
  3. Aberrant Organisms: trigger events, very aggressive, high profit.
  4. Leviathan-Class Entities: not meant to be farmed; environmental threats; change weather; pull boats. (See Leviathan (Godblood Zone).)

Environmental storytelling (ChatGPT suggestions)

At high Endro levels fewer NPCs are visible · some days docks are emptier · a boat doesn't come back.

Ideas

  • single-player, co-op and local servers up to 24 (see "Players and platforms").
  • Events where the player sees a powerful human in action (ties to Endro and Society).

entries.summary: Conceptual.

Conceptual. Nothing here is canon. Follows Kalfu's Dominion Options. The author asked to compare all five Sovereigns at the same level of detail, with the ladder of the Diving Index from Ripple to Abyssal Crown. Examples illustrate possibility; real Edicts are invented by the bearer (Edicts).

The author's criteria so far: fights as a mobile skirmisher and a creative trickster; the costs that hurt most are being forgotten and distance from people; the Dominion should be opposite to what he believes he needs; the reader intuits the Sovereign early and it is confirmed at the end of Chapter 10.
